newsitem.title: USA: Congress returns to budget deficit ban showdown.
newsitem.headline: Congress returns to budget deficit ban showdown.

text.p: Republicans next week face a crucial Senate test for one of their top political goals, a constitutional ban on budget deficits, and their success hinges on two publicly uncommitted freshmen Democrats.

Fresh from a week's recess, Congress will also gear up for intense scrutiny of campaign fundraising by committees in both the House and Senate. And, President Bill Clinton is to continue battling for Senate accceptance of the remaining unconfirmed members of his second-term cabinet.

Republicans have long sought passage of a constitutional amendment to require the budget be balanced each year, and came within one vote of passage in 1995. At week's end, Democrats were one vote shy of the 34 votes needed to defeat it.

The outcome could be decided by Democrats Robert Toricelli of New Jersey and Mary Landrieu of Louisiana who had pledged support for the amendment during their campaigns but have not declared their intentions this year.

As in previous debates, the politically sensitive issue of Social Security retirement benefits seemed to be moving lawmakers to defeat the amendment. An important swing vote, Democratic Sen. Tim Johnson of South Dakota announced on Thursday that he would not back the amendment after seeing a report that suggested its passage could jeopardize Social Security benefits in the next century.

House Republican leaders were forced to hold the balanced budget amendment in the Judiciary Committee rather than go ahead with the Feb. 26 vote scheduled for the full House when it became clear that many Republicans also had concerns about Social Security. A Democratic plan to exempt Social Security may have had enough Republican support to pass the Judiciary panel, but no vote was held.

Republican supporters, led by Sen. Orrin Hatch of Utah, argued that the retirement benefits were not endangered and that the issue was a scare tactic raised by those intent upon the amendment's defeat. The amendment was sponsored by all 55 Republican senators and 7 Democrats.

Senate debate began on Feb. 5 and could conclude next week. Republicans argued that only the discipline of a constitutional amendment would force the tough decisions needed to cut the budget and end government red ink.

The amendment would require that the budget be balanced each year during peacetime, starting with 2002 or two years after ratification. It would force Congress to muster a three-fifths majority vote to permit deficits in any year. It would also make it harder for Congress to raise taxes.
To pass the amendment, a two-thirds vote of both the House and Senate is required, and then it must be ratified by 38 of 50 states within the next seven years.

The Senate next week will vote on a Democratic proposal to exempt Social Security from the budget calculation and later in the week on a Democratic substitute balanced budget amendment that would waive the amendment during economic hard times. Neither is expected to attract enough votes from the Republican majority to pass.

The balanced budget constitutional amendment has been debated thoroughly over many years but only once did it come close to approval. In 1995 a similar plan cleared the House but failed in the Senate by one vote.
It is opposed by President Clinton and by Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan.

In his weekly radio address, the president repeated his opposition. "We must balance the buget, but a balanced budget amendment could cause more harm than good," he said. Clinton said that the amendment could force the courts to cut benefits or raise taxes if necessary to meet the constitutional requirement of an annual balanced budget.

With an eye on Toricelli's pivotal vote, Republicans asked New Jersey's Rep. Bob Franks to rebuff the president. "That's outrageous. It's the worst form of demagoguery," Franks said in his party's radio address.
While budget battles take center stage in the Senate, the House is expected to approve a reinstatement of the 10 percent airline ticket tax next week. Senate approval is expected to follow quickly.

Campaign fund-raising comes under intense scrutiny in the House where investigators threatened to hold two former Clinton aides in contempt for failure to turn over documents. The two, John Huang and Webster Hubbell, cited their constitutional right to not incriminate themselves.

The Senate probe got under way with the issuance of 54 subpoenas, 52 of which were to those associated with Democratic campaigns. Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Fred Thompson, Republican of Tennessee, has expanded the investigation to include both congressional and presidential campaigns.

Clinton vowed on Friday to stand by his selection for Labor Secretary, White House aide Alexis Herman, whose nomination has run into trouble in the Republican-controlled Senate. Some Republicans questioned whether she violated the law when her office invited a federal banking regulator to a political coffee meeting at the White House with Clinton and bankers. Labor Committee Chairman Jim Jeffords, Republican of Vermont, said he does not want to schedule her hearing until the issue is resolved.
Anthony Lake, Clinton's choice to head the Central Intelligence Agency, will answer his opponents early next month in hearings of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
